doc.title: Jay Leonhart interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: How he began writing songs and performing them himself
summary: He wrote limericks in high school and later songs including a 1973-74 gas shortage song, and always planned to perform his own songs, including an upcoming off-Broadway show.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When did you first get into — have an urge to do your own songs?

Well I wrote poetry in high school as a sort of a way to communicate to friends and have fun. And I found out I could write a limerick pretty easy, it’s not that hard to do, the English language does have some rhymes in it, and if you think about it you can find them. Then in the 30s, all of a sudden I just — the kids were born and I wrote a sort of a Sesame Street song that I liked. A little silly and sappy and all that kind of stuff, but I liked it. Then we had a big gasoline shortage I think in ‘73 or ‘74, I mean a big one. And I wrote, “I’m thirteenth in line at the filling station/Waiting to pick up my weekly ration/Of gasoline/From a big machine.” And I wrote a country song that actually got a little bit of airplay in the country, in the east. And I had a lot of fun putting it together and enjoyed the little bit of publicity and I said you know this publicity can help you in your music career. I said it can really not be a bad thing. You can get work, people know your name, and you might work in all sort of peripheral areas, even as a jazz bassist. So pursuing and promoting the songs was not something I didn’t want to do. I loved writing them, thought it was something, the challenge, the fun of actually performing the songs, that you can actually earn a living at it, it’s very expressive and everything, I mean it just became like a hobby that I really loved pursuing and felt very good when I was doing it. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -11-
And what about the first time you decided you could deliver them yourself?

Well I automatically assumed I was going to deliver them myself. I didn’t think anybody was going to do them for me. I never even thought that I would be a songwriter for other people. I thought whatever level I achieve at this, I will do it, I will perform my own music, and anyone who hears them and wants to do them is free to do them. And as a result I have not spent any time, comparatively speaking, promoting my own music, which is a mistake in terms of economic, although I have survived economically so maybe it’s not such a big mistake. I didn’t get rich. If that’s a sin well then that’s the sin. But I do work consistently on it. I’ve got a show coming up on Broadway this fall, I’ll be in it, an off-Broadway, and hopefully it will move up to Broadway. We’ll see what level we’re going to get it to, but it’s seriously produced, of all my own music, just a story weave through which I’ve taken a list of about 150 songs that I’ve written and then picked the ones that I really love, that have something to say, that are funny, that are poignant, that to my way of thinking have something to say — excuse me as I bang the mic again. That have something to say, and turn them into a song with a little bit of chatter in between to sort of tie things together or maybe not. But it’s easy to sort of find a way of weaving and not make it so totally self centered you know, but it’s about the world, life, science, photon splitting and all kinds of songs. I mean I have a lot of songs. And we’ve done a couple of run throughs of it — or is it runs through — run throughs or runs through. Oh I figured out something the other day. Now did you know that the word “the” should be pronounced “thee” probably in front of a vowel and “the” in front of a consonant.
